ceb.title: How Canonization Works
ceb.question: How does the Church 'make' saints, and can it be wrong when it declares someone a saint?
ceb.answer: Canonization does not make a person holy; it is the Church's solemn recognition that a person is already in heaven and may be venerated by the universal Church and invoked as an intercessor. The process is rigorous: after a waiting period, the person's life and writings are examined for heroic virtue, earning the title Venerable, then beatification (title Blessed) normally requires one verified miracle attributed to their intercession, and canonization requires a second, medically inexplicable miracle. These miracles serve as God's own confirmation from heaven. Because Scripture calls all the faithful 'saints' (Rom 1:7) and pictures the martyrs alive before God (Rev 6:9-11), the Church simply identifies specific witnesses for imitation. Many theologians hold that formal canonization engages the Church's infallibility, since it would be gravely misleading to command the universal veneration of someone not truly saved; thus the Church trusts it cannot err in this solemn act.

en.answer_full:
> "For all the saints who from their labors rest, who thee by faith before the world confessed, thy name, O Jesus, be forever blest: Alleluia!"
> — Ancient Church antiphon (William Walsham How, 1864 versification)

The Catholic process of canonization is simultaneously the most rigorous, the most misunderstood, and the most theologically profound aspect of the Church's life that most Catholics know little about. It is not a political process for declaring popular figures divine. It is a careful, multi-century, multi-stage examination of whether a specific person lived the Christian life to a heroic degree — and whether God himself, through miracles, has confirmed that this person now intercedes from heaven. Understanding the process requires understanding what the Church is actually claiming: not that she makes people holy, but that she recognizes what God has already done.

---

## The Theological Foundation

### What Is a Saint?

The New Testament uses the Greek *hagioi* — "holy ones" or "saints" — to refer to all baptized Christians who are members of the Body of Christ:

- *"To all the beloved of God in Rome, called to be holy"* (Romans 1:7, NABRE)
- *"To the church of God that is in Corinth, to you who have been sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be holy"* (1 Corinthians 1:2, NABRE)

Every Christian is called to be a saint. Canonization is the recognition that a specific person answered this call to its fullest degree — not merely living a good Christian life, but exercising the theological and cardinal virtues at a "heroic" level throughout their life.

### Scriptural Basis for Heavenly Intercession

The canonization process assumes that the saints in heaven intercede for those on earth:

*"Each of the elders held a harp and gold bowls filled with incense, which are the prayers of the holy ones."* (Revelation 5:8, NABRE)

*"Another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a gold censer. He was given a great quantity of incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the holy ones."* (Revelation 8:3, NABRE)

The saints in heaven present the prayers of those on earth before God's throne. A canonized saint is one the Church has formally recognized as being in that company — able to intercede on our behalf.

---

## The Four Stages of Canonization

### Stage 1: Servant of God — Diocesan Inquiry

- Must be at least 5 years after death (Pope can waive this — as with Mother Teresa, beatified 6 years after death)
- The local bishop opens a formal inquiry into the candidate's life, virtues, and writings
- All writings are examined for theological error
- Witnesses are interviewed; documents gathered
- If the diocese determines heroic virtue is plausible, the case is forwarded to the **Dicastery for the Causes of Saints** in Rome
- The person is given the title **Servant of God**

### Stage 2: Venerable — Confirmation of Heroic Virtue

- Roman theologians examine the diocesan inquiry in depth
- Cardinals and bishops of the Dicastery vote on whether the evidence demonstrates **heroic virtue** — the theological virtues (faith, hope, charity) and cardinal virtues (prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance) practiced at an exceptional, sustained level
- If the Pope approves, he issues a decree declaring the person **Venerable**
- No miracle is required at this stage

### Stage 3: Beatification — First Miracle

- One verified miracle is required (attributed to the candidate's intercession after death)
- For martyrs: beatification may proceed without a miracle if martyrdom is confirmed
- The miracle process involves:
  - Medical documentation of the healing
  - Review by the Consulta Medica (independent physicians, including non-Catholics)
  - Determination that the healing is "scientifically inexplicable"
  - Theological review confirming the healing was attributed to the candidate's intercession
- Upon beatification, the person receives the title **Blessed** and may be venerated locally or by a specific religious institute

### Stage 4: Canonization — Second Miracle and Universal Proclamation

- A second miracle after beatification is required
- The same rigorous medical and theological review applies
- The Pope canonizes the Blessed in a solemn ceremony, declaring:
  - The person is definitively in heaven
  - Their feast day is added to the universal calendar
  - The whole Church may venerate them and invoke their intercession

| Stage | Title | Requirement |
|-------|-------|-------------|
| Diocesan inquiry | Servant of God | Death, initial investigation |
| Vatican decree | Venerable | Confirmed heroic virtue |
| Beatification | Blessed | 1 verified miracle (or martyrdom) |
| Canonization | Saint | 2nd verified miracle |

---

## The Role of Miracles

The miracle requirement is theologically significant, not bureaucratic. It represents God's own testimony that the candidate is with him in glory. The Church does not canonize on human judgment alone — she waits for a divine sign. The medical review is designed to establish that the healing exceeds natural explanation, making supernatural causation the most credible explanation.

The Consulta Medica applies rigorous criteria:
1. The disease or condition must be serious and well-documented
2. The healing must be instantaneous or rapid, not gradual
3. The healing must be complete and permanent
4. There must be no medical explanation — not merely an unlikely outcome, but a genuinely inexplicable one
5. The healing must be linked in time and intention to prayer invoking the candidate's intercession

---

## Church Fathers on the Saints

> "We offer sacrifices for the dead on their birthdays. We consider that day the birthday of those martyrs — and indeed their birthday — because on it they were born to eternal life."
> — Tertullian, *On the Crown* (De Corona), 3 (c. 211 AD)

The early Church commemorated martyrs on the anniversary of their death — treating it as their birthday into heaven and gathering at their graves to celebrate the Eucharist. This is the oldest form of canonization: the Church's local recognition that these individuals are in heaven.

> "Stephen was stoned, and he prayed for those who were stoning him. It is a great thing to pray for enemies. But now that he is with Christ, shall he not do this more effectively?"
> — St. Augustine of Hippo, *Sermon 315* (c. 420 AD)

Augustine's logic grounds the entire theology of saintly intercession: if Stephen prayed for his killers while dying, how much more effectively does he intercede for us now that he is in Christ's presence in glory?

---

## CCC References

| Reference | Teaching |
|-----------|----------|
| CCC 828 | The Church canonizes: declares with certainty those who lived heroic virtue are in glory |
| CCC 946 | The communion of saints — the sharing of holy things among holy people |
| CCC 956 | The saints intercede for us and the merits of Christ are applied through their prayers |
| CCC 2683 | The saints contemplate God and intercede for those on earth |

---

## Common Objections

**"The Bible says only God is holy — calling people saints is presumptuous."**

The New Testament applies *hagioi* (saints, holy ones) to living Christians throughout the epistles (Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:2, Ephesians 1:1). Canonization is the Church formally recognizing that the holiness God calls all Christians to has been achieved heroically in a specific person. It does not compete with God's holiness — it proclaims it, as manifested in a human life.

**"Canonization is a medieval invention — the early Church didn't do this."**

The early Church did canonize — by popular acclamation, especially of martyrs. Local calendar entries recording a martyr's feast day were the earliest form. The process became centralized and formalized (first formal papal canonization: 993 AD) as the Church grew. But the underlying theology — recognizing martyrs and confessors as in heaven, invoking their intercession — is universal from the first century.

**"The miracle requirement is superstitious."**

The miracle requirement is the Church's insistence that she not act on human enthusiasm alone. By requiring a medically documented, independently reviewed, scientifically inexplicable healing attributed to the candidate's intercession, the Church submits her judgment to God's own confirmation. It is the opposite of superstition — it is methodological humility before the divine.

---

The canonization process is one of the most humanly demanding and theologically rigorous procedures in the institutional life of any religion. It takes decades. It requires independent medical verification of events that cannot be naturally explained. It subjects the candidate's entire written legacy to theological scrutiny. At the end, it proclaims something specific and joyful: God's grace won. A human being, with all the fragility of our nature, cooperated with divine grace so completely that they now stand in the presence of God — and from that presence, pray for us.
